note.note:
Consult Summary:
- 27-year-old man with 3 days of profuse watery diarrhea, occurring approximately hourly while awake, with intermittent crampy lower central abdominal pain and associated nausea/vomiting.
- Impression given by clinician: probable acute gastroenteritis; advised oral rehydration (Diarolyte OTC), fluids/soft diet, paracetamol PRN, avoidance of alcohol, and to recontact if not improving within 48 hours or if signs of dehydration.

Problem List:

Issue 1: Acute watery diarrhea (suspected gastroenteritis)
- Timeline and symptoms: 3 days of profuse watery stools, occurring roughly every hour when awake; stools described as very loose/“pouring straight” from the rectum.
- Associated symptoms: intermittent crampy lower central abdominal pain (comes and goes), subjective feverishness/hot sensation, reduced urine frequency.
- Systems review / pertinent negatives: denies visible blood in stool; reports nausea and some vomiting (see Issue 2); no measured temperature recorded.
- Social / exposure: brother had similar symptoms for ~5 days and may be a potential contact.
- Examination findings: no formal physical examination or vital signs documented.
- Differential / clinician impression: clinician suspected gastroenteritis and advised conservative management.

Issue 2: Nausea and vomiting
- Timeline and symptoms: nausea present since onset; at least one episode of vomiting after intake of milk.
- Relation to diet: patient reports vomiting triggered by milk on at least one occasion.
- Severity: vomiting described as less prominent than diarrhea.
- Medications/management: advised paracetamol for fever/pain (paracetamol taken recently by patient; dose/route/frequency not documented).

Issue 3: Dehydration risk and functional impact
- Features suggesting dehydration risk: high stool frequency (~hourly), subjective feeling of being very hot, reduced urine frequency.
- Functional impact: difficulty managing at work; prefers not to take time off work; lives with mother and sister (brother does not live with him).
- Social history relevant to management: occasional social smoker; consumes alcohol with heavier drinking episodes 1–2 times/month — clinician advised avoiding alcohol while unwell.

Medications:
- Paracetamol — dose/route/frequency not documented (patient has taken recently for symptoms).
- Diarolyte (oral rehydration solution) recommended — dose/route/frequency not documented; OTC (no prescription required).

Allergies:
- No known drug allergies reported.

Past Medical History:
- Patient reports otherwise “fit and well”; no chronic medical conditions disclosed.

Social History:
- Lives with mother and sister; brother does not live with him and has had similar illness.
- Occupation: office-based work in central London (government).
- Smoking: social smoker (not regular; typically on social occasions).
- Alcohol: occasional; heavier drinking 1–2 times per month.
- Prefers not to take time off work.

Preventative History:
- No preventative care, screening, or vaccination history discussed in this consult.

Physical Examination:
- No vital signs documented.
- No clinician-performed physical examination findings recorded.
- Patient-reported findings: intermittent crampy lower central abdominal pain (pain severity ~6/10 when present), subjective feverishness, reduced urine frequency.

Plan:
- Conservative management for presumed gastroenteritis:
  - Maintain hydration with clear fluids.
  - Use oral rehydration solution (Diarolyte) available OTC to replace fluids/electrolytes.
  - Soft diet as tolerated (soup, mashed foods) and gradually advance as tolerated.
  - Paracetamol as needed for fever or pain (dose/route/frequency not documented).
  - Avoid alcohol while unwell.
- Safety net / follow-up:
  - Recontact clinician if symptoms do not settle within 48 hours.
  - Seek assessment earlier if signs of dehydration develop (e.g., markedly reduced urine output, dizziness, persistent vomiting) — clinician advised further investigation if dehydrated.
  - Planned check on progress in 1–2 days per clinician’s advice.

Document_quality (quality checks):
- Missing but clinically expected elements:
  - Objective vital signs (temperature, pulse, blood pressure, respiratory rate).
  - Formal abdominal and dehydration-focused physical examination.
  - Quantified stool frequency/output and urine output measurements.
  - Laboratory or stool testing (e.g., electrolytes, renal function, stool culture) not performed or discussed.
  - Specific paracetamol dosing guidance not recorded.
- Internal conflicts from the transcript:
  - No direct clinical contradictions identified. (Minor conversational irregularities and brief unclear utterances present; physician briefly said “you’re feeling hoarse” though patient did not report hoarseness.)
- Transcript quality:
  - Audio/video connection issues noted at start; occasional brief unclear or overlapping speech, but overall history and plan were understandable.
